extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially those writing person-vs-nature / survival / milieu stories)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical criteria for crafting stories where the natural setting functions as the antagonist (survival, disaster, endemic, or milieu stories). Focuses on plotting, pacing, character goals, research, and devices for making environment-driven conflict compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do your research
rubrics_metrics.description: Do your research. Because... the more research you do, the cooler your story is going to get.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn real survival/disaster/environmental details so you can plausibly present things that go wrong and interesting solutions. Research suggests 'a thousand cooler things' to use as obstacles or inventive fixes. Anti-pattern: relying on obvious mistakes readers knowledgeable about the milieu (the 'Boy Scout in the room') will immediately spot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting must function as an antagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature is serving the function of the antagonist, stopping the protagonist from achieving some goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure the protagonist has a clear goal that the environment is preventing them from reaching. If the setting doesn't actively impede a goal, the conflict will feel flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define protagonist goals and plateaus
rubrics_metrics.description: There are often plateaus of goals for the protagonist to achieve; the protagonist's goal is allowed to change more frequently and more completely than normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the story around smaller, achievable objectives (shelter, water, signaling) that create a sense of progress and provide natural beats for reassessment and escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milieu (MICE) structure: entry → exit
rubrics_metrics.description: Person versus nature, in MICE terms, is a milieu story, with the goal of getting out of the milieu, or at least navigating and surviving it. Start with entry into the milieu, end with exit from the milieu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the story's beginning as the character entering a place and the ending as their exit; all conflicts are obstacles to that exit. Homework exercise: pick a milieu, a starting point, and an exit; brainstorm ~20 things preventing exit; pick your five favorites and rank them by difficulty to structure escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation and reaction of the environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Make things worse and worse even as the protagonist levels up; the antagonist (nature) should react and escalate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unanticipated consequences of the character's choices to ratchet tension. Example: flooding an area to stop fire ants but creating new hazards. Nature should appear to 'react' to the protagonist's actions, increasing stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the familiar unfamiliar
rubrics_metrics.description: Something familiar becomes unfamiliar — that shift is what makes the setting disturbing and interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take an everyday location or expectation and invert or alter it (e.g., an upside-down cruise ship) so readers can recognize but be unsettled by it. This principle drives both horror and survival tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropomorphize environmental elements for rivalry/showdown
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropomorphized elements of the environment can function as villain-like rivals leading to showdowns (e.g., octopus, tooth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build up fear or rivalry toward a natural feature or creature over the course of the story so a confrontation feels earned and cathartic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person-vs-nature can be a time-bomb or puzzle/mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes nature is a time bomb. In science fiction settings, the resolution often has a sense-of-wonder reveal — it becomes a mystery or puzzle-box story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your environmental conflict is primarily survival (skills and endurance), a ticking disaster (time pressure), or a puzzle (discovering how the environment works). In SF, emphasize revelation and wonder rather than only brute survival techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use person-vs-nature as arc or subplot where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: You can use person versus nature as one arc or subplot in a story rather than the whole novel; antagonists can shift (e.g., island → boys).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider making environmental conflict one thread among others so the novel doesn't become monotonous. Allow the antagonist to change over time (environment → human society) for thematic depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a character who verbalizes the nature principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Having a character who gives voice to the nature/chaos principle (e.g., Dr. Malcolm) helps events feel like natural consequences rather than 'author picking worst thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an in-world explainer or skeptic to frame why systems fail or why the environment behaves a certain way; this makes subsequent problems feel inevitable and believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply want/need/get triad to the environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat nature like an antagonist with 'want, need, get' being possibly different things to create twists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the environment's apparent motive, need, and actual outcome differ, that can produce meaningful irony or thematic payoff (e.g., what nature 'wanted' vs. what it 'needed').

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan sense-of-wonder resolutions in SF
rubrics_metrics.description: In science fiction person-versus-nature, often the resolution is a wonder reveal about how the alien environment really works rather than just a craft-skill solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the mystery and the reveal early so the landing feels satisfying; map the reveal to character learning/discovery rather than chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time emotional beats using the environment's structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing how person versus nature works helps you time emotional punches — the environment can govern pacing and key emotional beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the milestones of survival (loss, small victories, resource depletion, confrontation) as timing anchors for emotional arcs. Plateaus of achievement make good moments for reflection or recalibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'Boy Scout' anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Be smarter than the Boy Scout in the room. Don't let the story begin with obvious competence that robs tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either justify why characters lack survival knowledge or provide fresh, non-trivial challenges that make common skills insufficient. Readers with real-world knowledge should not be able to easily predict or fix the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use unanticipated consequences as tension drivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Find environmental things that throw up barriers, especially unanticipated consequences of decisions the character makes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design cause → unexpected effect sequences (e.g., solution A creates hazard B). These are effective ways to escalate stakes and keep conflict dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure obstacles and rank for escalating difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Brainstorm about twenty things preventing the character from exiting; rank your five favorites in order of difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exercise produces a ladder of obstacles you can use to pace escalation and ensure the protagonist faces increasingly hard challenges rather than a static threat level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ examples/resources to ground plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Use exemplar works and practical resources (e.g., Hatchet; How to Invent Everything) to learn structure, tone, and practical problem-solving you can adapt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read canonical person-vs-nature stories to see pacing and structure; consult practical guides (time-traveler cheat-sheets, survival manuals) to add believable detail and inventive solutions.
